summary:
Consensual same-sex relations have been legal in Tajikistan since May 1998, and sexual relations between women were never criminalised. The age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The formal legality does not carry through into protection: no legislation in Tajikistan prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

The country's first anti-discrimination law, adopted in July 2022, dropped sexual orientation and gender identity as protected grounds and retains only "sex". A regional monitoring review covering 2024 finds the statute only partially aligned with international standards, and an earlier comparative legislative analysis built from questionnaires completed by local partners records legal barriers and gaps affecting gay men, men who have sex with men and trans people, including cases where the written law protects but practice does not.

Authorities maintain a register of LGBT people. Police introduced it in 2016, and Outright International flags a 2017 government registry of "proven" LGBT persons. ILGA-Europe's annual review for 2024 reports that police lure LGBT people into fake meetings in order to register them in a database, harvest their social-media contacts and extort money, with more than ten such cases recorded in Sughd province.

Policing is the documented source of the acute risk. IPHR's report of February 2024 records police raids in 2022 and 2023 that brought forced HIV testing and arbitrary criminal charges, together with documented ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by officers. ECOM recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people during 2024, including arbitrary arrest, blackmail and extortion. ILGA-Europe further reports that forced or sham marriages are used against LGBT people with police declining to intervene.

Legal gender recognition is blocked in practice. Tajik law permits reassignment on some documents, but medical institutions issue no official documents for that purpose. A diagnosis of transsexualism is required, surgery is required for transgender women but not for transgender men, and evaluation is carried out by commissions of three psychiatrists on an unregulated case-by-case basis in which activists say bribes are often necessary. Only three to six people are known to have completed a legal gender change.

Gender-affirming medical services are not available in Tajikistan, so trans people who medically transition must travel abroad, and most doctors have no expertise in the treatments required. Patients report disrespectful treatment from medical staff, and some Tajik psychologists and doctors offer pseudoscientific methods that present homosexuality as an addiction comparable to alcoholism or drug addiction.

The wider social climate constrains visibility. Public expression of support for LGBT people is effectively suppressed and public attitudes have been described as entirely negative, with homophobic and transphobic remarks from politicians forming part of everyday politics. The Supreme Mufti, Saidmukarram Abdulkodirzoda, has called same-sex relations a "disaster", condemned countries legalising same-sex marriage, and spoken against human-rights activists and anti-discrimination laws. Those who disclose their orientation become targets of physical and psychological abuse, including at the hands of police.

No relationship-recognition framework exists in Tajikistan, and same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to married heterosexual couples.
tangentialFactors:
The legal position sits inside a broader pattern of state repression rather than a targeted statute alone. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2017 describes a sharp deterioration in Tajikistan during 2016, with opposition leadership sentenced, human-rights lawyers imprisoned and a predetermined referendum extending presidential rule.

Social hostility long predates the police registry. Reporting from January 2013, fifteen years after decriminalisation, describes very little tolerance and one of the most closed LGBT communities in the region, with physical and psychological abuse following disclosure.

ECOM's 2024 study on trans people's access to medical services, including HIV prevention and treatment and hormone replacement therapy across the eastern Europe and central Asia region, has a Tajikistan country coordinator contributing and carries guidance aimed at trans migrants. In country, a trans-focused non-governmental organisation has drafted a hormone-replacement-therapy protocol used to educate endocrinologists.

The repressive context also affects detainee reporting generally: Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 chapter on Tajikistan addresses prison and detention only in relation to opposition figures and deportees, which limits what can be concluded about conditions for detained LGBT people.
localsOnly:
LGBT groups in Tajikistan operate anonymously. One focuses solely on trans issues and one on general LGBT issues, and activists have no access to the Ministry of Health or other state authorities, which makes state-level advocacy impossible.

The 2016 police register and the 2017 registry of "proven" LGBT persons fall on residents rather than visitors. Forced or sham marriage is reported as a pressure mechanism applied to LGBT people in their own communities, with police inaction recorded alongside it.

Because no domestic provider performs gender-affirming procedures, residents who transition medically must go abroad for care, and the absence of official documentation from medical institutions means legal gender change cannot be completed domestically. A diagnosis of transsexualism, psychiatric commission evaluation and, for transgender women, surgery remain prerequisites, with only three to six successful cases recorded.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records the placement or conditions of trans detainees in Tajikistan; Human Rights Watch's 2025 chapter does not cover them, so that question is unresolved rather than answered.

The inventory contains no findings on LGBT minors, education-sector policies or school environments in Tajikistan.

Entry, visa and border-document screening rules for trans travellers are not sourced here, so whether identity documents are checked for gender markers on arrival is unresolved. Whether the police registry is accessible to or applied against foreign visitors is also not established by these sources.

It is not sourced whether the July 2022 anti-discrimination law has been invoked in any proceeding, and no enforcement data on that statute appears in the inventory.
